segments.title: HMS Tiger and the battlecruiser trade-off
segments.summary: HMS Tiger shows how British battlecruisers pursued heavy guns and 28-knot speed while accepting less protection than a battleship.
segments.body: Tiger's 13.5-inch guns fit the same capital-ship environment as the contemporary Iron Duke and Queen Elizabeth programmes. The weapon was already standard among Britain's latest battleships. Tiger remained a battlecruiser, while the Queen Elizabeths were fast battleships. Her machinery, served by 39 water-tube boilers, produced 85,000 shaft horsepower for a top speed of 28 knots, and the spacing around the after guns left useful room. Her belt resembled those of other British battlecruisers because the design placed speed and firepower ahead of armour. This balance defined both her tactical promise and the limits of what such ships could safely do in fleet action.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses Tiger's guns, boilers, speed, armour belt, and British battlecruiser priorities.

segments.title: Normandie's quadruple-turret compromise
segments.summary: France's Normandie class concentrated twelve 13.4-inch guns in quadruple turrets, but its 21-knot speed and unusual layout raised hard questions about the design's value.
segments.body: Normandie illustrates how a larger broadside could still produce an unconvincing battleship. The design packed twelve 13.4-inch guns into three quadruple turrets, including an unusual aft-facing concentration that made the layout visually and tactically awkward. Its broadside invited comparison with Italian battleships carrying thirteen 12-inch guns, though raw gun count could flatter an awkward design. At 21 knots, Normandie was slow beside the fast British designs in the episode, while its armour was compared with French and German battlecruiser protection. Béarn, the only hull that entered service, did so as an aircraft carrier. Even in that poor carrier form, she was probably more useful than the battleship would have been. Since none of the class entered service as a battleship, the design also shows the limits of paper comparison.

evidence.note: The transcript examines Normandie's quadruple turrets, gun count, Italian broadside comparison, speed, protection, and uncompleted service history.

segments.title: Pennsylvania's twelve-gun answer
segments.summary: The Pennsylvania class used four triple 14-inch turrets to offer a heavier broadside than a Queen Elizabeth without waiting for a new gun or turret design.
segments.body: The Pennsylvania class developed technology the United States already had in hand. Four triple turrets replaced the earlier mix of triple and twin mounts, giving the ship twelve 14-inch guns against the Queen Elizabeth class's eight 15-inch guns. Existing weapons and turret designs made Pennsylvania a swift, practical answer. Its 21.38-knot speed still left the Queen Elizabeths with an advantage in open water. Pennsylvania's powerful broadside posed a different tactical problem if confined waters restricted the faster British ships' manoeuvre. The knight-and-rook analogy makes the geometry concrete: agility offers choices in open space, while a powerful line of fire dominates when movement is constrained.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the Pennsylvania class's four triple 14-inch turrets, broadside, existing turret technology, speed trade-off, and knight-and-rook tactical analogy.

segments.title: Bayern, Revenge, and fleet numbers
segments.summary: Comparing the Bayern and Revenge classes shows why capital-ship competition involved speed, armour, gun calibre, and the number of hulls a navy could afford.
segments.body: Matching Queen Elizabeth's eight 15-inch guns at roughly 21 knots still left Bayern short of the faster British ship's tactical freedom. Bayern looked formidable on paper but was closer to the Revenge class than to the Queen Elizabeths. The American decision to retain 14-inch guns also spared Britain from an immediate technical escalation and let it emphasize hull numbers. Revenge could carry eight 15-inch guns and a 13-inch belt, while Bayern's quoted belt varied from 6.7 to 13.8 inches. Revenge's shorter, more crowded hull also appeared to offer less room for later improvement than Queen Elizabeth. Cheaper twin mounts supported Britain's preference for a larger fleet over more ambitious multiple-gun installations.

evidence.note: The transcript compares the German response, Queen Elizabeth and Revenge classes, American gun choices, armour, speed, and turret cost.

segments.title: Salamis and the limits of international supply
segments.summary: The unfinished Salamis reveals how a warship programme could be stranded when hull construction, heavy guns, and international supply chains did not align.
segments.body: Salamis was under construction in Germany while its heavy guns depended on American delivery, leaving a critical vulnerability once war intervened. Germany lacked the industrial capacity to build both the hull and the guns. The project therefore depended on several countries even though the hull itself looked promising. Industrial capacity and international access to armament separated an impressive design from a completed fighting ship. The undelivered guns may later have armed Abercrombie-class monitors. If so, that use shows how wartime needs could redirect scarce equipment.

evidence.note: The transcript explains that Salamis depended on American guns and connects the undelivered armament to Abercrombie-class monitors.

segments.title: Why the 1913 naval race was global
segments.summary: The 1913 capital-ship race reached far beyond Britain and Germany, with American, Japanese, Spanish, French, and other programmes shaping the wider contest.
segments.body: Several navies were developing ships and technologies at the same time, making the dreadnought race much wider than a British-German contest. In the 1913 snapshot, Britain is accelerating, Germany is trying to catch up, Spain has a ship in the water, the United States and Japan are doing well, and France is pursuing its own awkward path. The competition concerned both hull counts and the ability to build an effective capital ship for a navy's particular strategic needs. Tiger's mission reached beyond a North Sea duel. British battlecruisers were meant to protect worldwide trade and hunt enemy cruisers and battlecruisers. Those different missions help explain each navy's choices about speed, armament, and purpose.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies the multinational character of the race and explains Tiger's global trade-protection role.

segments.title: A technology race, not only a hull race
segments.summary: Pennsylvania shows how dreadnought competition rewarded qualitative design escalation even when fleets were not matching one another hull for hull.
segments.body: Pennsylvania appears as a simple, understated response to Britain's latest capital ships. Britain was the only navy building ships that justified an American battleship with twelve 14-inch guns. The competition therefore extended beyond laying down more hulls. It was also a technology and design race over who could build the best battleship. This distinction explains why qualitative escalation mattered even when fleets pursued different global ambitions.

evidence.note: The transcript calls Pennsylvania an understated response and distinguishes a technology and design race from a simple race to build more ships.

segments.title: American deterrence without escalation
segments.summary: Pennsylvania combined regional deterrence with a 12-gun broadside, while British and American firms still shared key turbine and boiler ideas.
segments.body: The American programme asserted naval status and regional security while responding in part to South American battleship construction. Brazil, Chile, and Argentina help explain why the United States could consider powerful battleships necessary in its own hemisphere without presenting the fleet as a global challenge to Britain. Turbine and boiler designs also moved between British and American firms while the two fleets were being compared. The Queen Elizabeths remained faster, but Pennsylvania's twelve 14-inch guns made it a ship no opponent could dismiss. The design offered credible American deterrence without an immediate leap to still larger guns.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses American regional naval status, South American programmes, technology exchange, and Pennsylvania's 12-gun deterrent.

segments.title: Why matching gun power did not equal deterrence
segments.summary: Bayern's eight 15-inch guns looked impressive in isolation, but a mixed British force could combine Revenge-class staying power with Queen Elizabeth-class speed.
segments.body: Bayern provides the contrast: equal headline armament did not produce equal strategic effect. Eight 15-inch guns and 21 knots looked comparable to British ships on paper, but the German design lacked the Queen Elizabeth class's speed. In a fleet action, Revenge-class battleships could hold or pin the German line while faster Queen Elizabeths manoeuvred around it. That movement raised the possibility of turning or crossing the German T. Deterrence therefore depended on fleet composition and tactical options as well as the gun count of a single class.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Bayern's paper armament with British speed, pinning by Revenge-class ships, and a Queen Elizabeth-class flanking threat.

segments.title: Capital ships and the uncertainty of deterrence
segments.summary: By 1913, fleets were ordering powerful ships to deter rivals without knowing how soon war would test whether their force was strong enough.
segments.body: Britain's planned Queen Elizabeth and Revenge construction promised a formidable concentration of 15-inch-gun battleships, but every navy still faced uncertainty about future threats. Six planned Queen Elizabeths and eight ordered Revenges could have amounted to fourteen such ships. That prospect could alarm rivals, yet navies ordering ships in 1913 did not know how close the next war was. They believed they had time and that their programmes were winning the deterrence contest. Deterrence depended on whether a fleet appeared powerful enough to keep a crisis from becoming a war.

evidence.note: The transcript connects planned British 15-inch battleships with the uncertainty of pre-war deterrence and approaching conflict.
